At Entertain Lawyers (www.entertainlawyers.com), we are fully committed to respecting and protecting your privacy. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your information.

1. Information we collect

We may collect the following types of information from you:

  • Personal Information : When you contact us or subscribe, we may ask for details such as your name, email address, and phone number.

  • Non-personal information : Browser type, device information, pages visited, and time spent on the website may be tracked so that we can improve the service.

2. Use of information

We may use your information for the following purposes:

  • To answer your questions

  • To send updates, newsletters, or promotional materials (only if you have subscribed)

  • To improve website functionality

  • To show targeted advertising or sponsored content

3. Sharing of information

We do not sell or share your personal information with third parties , except:

  • In case of legal obligation

  • With service providers who assist in operating the website (under their confidentiality agreement)

4. Cookies

Our website uses cookies to improve your experience and analyze traffic. You can disable cookies through your browser settings.

5. Data Security

We use industry-standard measures to protect your personal information. However, the Internet is not completely secure, so we cannot guarantee absolute security.

6. Third-party links

Our website may contain links to external websites. We are not responsible for the privacy policies of those websites.

7. Children's privacy

Our website is not intended for children under the age of 13. We do not knowingly collect information from such minors.

8. Change in policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. Any changes will be posted on this page.

9. Contact us

If you have any questions about this Privacy Policy, please contact us:

📧 इमेल: contact@entertainlawyers.com
📱 फोन: +977-98XXXXXXXX

Who we are

Suggested text: Our website address is: https://entertainlawyers.com.

Comments

Suggested text: When visitors leave comments on the site we collect the data shown in the comments form, and also the visitor’s IP address and browser user agent string to help spam detection.

An anonymized string created from your email address (also called a hash) may be provided to the Gravatar service to see if you are using it. The Gravatar service privacy policy is available here: https://automattic.com/privacy/. After approval of your comment, your profile picture is visible to the public in the context of your comment.

Media

Suggested text: If you upload images to the website, you should avoid uploading images with embedded location data (EXIF GPS) included. Visitors to the website can download and extract any location data from images on the website.

Cookies

Suggested text: If you leave a comment on our site you may opt-in to saving your name, email address and website in cookies. These are for your convenience so that you do not have to fill in your details again when you leave another comment. These cookies will last for one year.

If you visit our login page, we will set a temporary cookie to determine if your browser accepts cookies. This cookie contains no personal data and is discarded when you close your browser.

When you log in, we will also set up several cookies to save your login information and your screen display choices. Login cookies last for two days, and screen options cookies last for a year. If you select "Remember Me", your login will persist for two weeks. If you log out of your account, the login cookies will be removed.

If you edit or publish an article, an additional cookie will be saved in your browser. This cookie includes no personal data and simply indicates the post ID of the article you just edited. It expires after 1 day.

Embedded content from other websites

Suggested text: Articles on this site may include embedded content (e.g. videos, images, articles, etc.). Embedded content from other websites behaves in the exact same way as if the visitor has visited the other website.

These websites may collect data about you, use cookies, embed additional third-party tracking, and monitor your interaction with that embedded content, including tracking your interaction with the embedded content if you have an account and are logged in to that website.

Who we share your data with

Suggested text: If you request a password reset, your IP address will be included in the reset email.

How long we retain your data

Suggested text: If you leave a comment, the comment and its metadata are retained indefinitely. This is so we can recognize and approve any follow-up comments automatically instead of holding them in a moderation queue.

For users that register on our website (if any), we also store the personal information they provide in their user profile. All users can see, edit, or delete their personal information at any time (except they cannot change their username). Website administrators can also see and edit that information.

What rights you have over your data

Suggested text: If you have an account on this site, or have left comments, you can request to receive an exported file of the personal data we hold about you, including any data you have provided to us. You can also request that we erase any personal data we hold about you. This does not include any data we are obliged to keep for administrative, legal, or security purposes.

Where your data is sent

Suggested text: Visitor comments may be checked through an automated spam detection service.

Entertain Lawyers is an online news portal published in both English and Nepali language, which publishes fair, factual and informative content related to law and legal matters. We aim to make citizens aware of the legal system, its development, and rights through reliable news and educational articles.

Our mission is to promote responsible journalism and be a trusted source of legal information for our readers. Whether it's court news, changes in legal policy, or educational content for law buffs—we always believe in fair and clear reporting.

Join us for reliable news, important discussions, and understanding Nepal's laws.

स्वतन्त्र समाचार माध्यमको रूपमा, पोखरिया खबर सत्यता, विश्वसनीयता, र निष्पक्षताको सिद्धान्तमा आधारित पत्रकारिता अभ्यास गर्छ। हामी हालका घटनाक्रम, सरकारी नीतिहरू, शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, व्यापार, संस्कृति, खेलकुद लगायत विभिन्न विषयहरू समेट्छौं, जसले हाम्रो पाठकहरूलाई आफ्नो दैनिक जीवनमा महत्त्वपूर्ण समाचारहरू बुझ्न सहयोग गर्छ।

हाम्रो प्रतिबद्ध पत्रकारहरूको टोली दिनरात मेहनत गरेर तपाईंलाई यथार्थपरक र प्रभावकारी समाचार उपलब्ध गराउने प्रयास गर्छ। हामी सत्यको रक्षा गर्दै स्थानीय समुदायको आवाजलाई सशक्त बनाउने लक्ष्य राख्छौं।

डिजिटल सञ्चार प्रविधिको प्रयोग गर्दै, पोखरिया खबर आफ्नो वेबसाइट र सामाजिक सञ्जालहरू मार्फत रियल-टाइम अपडेट, ब्रेकिङ न्यूज, र विस्तृत विश्लेषण प्रदान गर्छ।

हामी विश्वास गर्छौं कि सूचित समाज नै बलियो समाज हो। जनतासम्म सही सूचना पुर्‍याउने हाम्रो प्रयास निरन्तर रहनेछ। पोखरिया खबर पोखरिया नगरपालिका र पर्सा जिल्लावासीहरूको लागि भरोसायोग्य समाचार स्रोत बन्न प्रतिबद्ध छ।

पोखरिया खबर पोखरिया नगरपालिका र पर्सा जिल्लाका ताजा, सटीक, र भरपर्दो समाचारहरू प्रदान गर्ने एक विश्वसनीय अनलाइन समाचार पोर्टल हो। हाम्रो उद्देश्य जनतालाई सत्य, तथ्यमा आधारित, र समयसापेक्ष समाचारहरू उपलब्ध गराउनु हो, जसले स्थानीय घटना, सामाजिक विषयहरू, राजनीतिक परिवर्तनहरू, र समुदायका महत्वपूर्ण कथाहरू उजागर गर्छ।

स्वतन्त्र समाचार माध्यमको रूपमा, पोखरिया खबर सत्यता, विश्वसनीयता, र निष्पक्षताको सिद्धान्तमा आधारित पत्रकारिता अभ्यास गर्छ। हामी हालका घटनाक्रम, सरकारी नीतिहरू, शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, व्यापार, संस्कृति, खेलकुद लगायत विभिन्न विषयहरू समेट्छौं, जसले हाम्रो पाठकहरूलाई आफ्नो दैनिक जीवनमा महत्त्वपूर्ण समाचारहरू बुझ्न सहयोग गर्छ।

हाम्रो प्रतिबद्ध पत्रकारहरूको टोली दिनरात मेहनत गरेर तपाईंलाई यथार्थपरक र प्रभावकारी समाचार उपलब्ध गराउने प्रयास गर्छ। हामी सत्यको रक्षा गर्दै स्थानीय समुदायको आवाजलाई सशक्त बनाउने लक्ष्य राख्छौं।

डिजिटल सञ्चार प्रविधिको प्रयोग गर्दै, पोखरिया खबर आफ्नो वेबसाइट र सामाजिक सञ्जालहरू मार्फत रियल-टाइम अपडेट, ब्रेकिङ न्यूज, र विस्तृत विश्लेषण प्रदान गर्छ।

हामी विश्वास गर्छौं कि सूचित समाज नै बलियो समाज हो। जनतासम्म सही सूचना पुर्‍याउने हाम्रो प्रयास निरन्तर रहनेछ। पोखरिया खबर पोखरिया नगरपालिका र पर्सा जिल्लावासीहरूको लागि भरोसायोग्य समाचार स्रोत बन्न प्रतिबद्ध छ।

पोखरिया खबर पोखरिया नगरपालिका र पर्सा जिल्लाको लोकप्रिय अनलाइन समाचार पोर्टल हो, जसमा हजारौँ स्थानीय पाठकहरू दैनिक रूपमा समाचार पढ्छन्। यदि तपाईं आफ्नो व्यवसाय, सेवा, वा उत्पादनको प्रचार गर्न चाहनुहुन्छ भने, पोखरिया खबर सबैभन्दा प्रभावकारी डिजिटल प्लेटफर्म हो।

हामीले प्रदान गर्ने विज्ञापन सेवाहरू:

✅ ब्यानर विज्ञापन: हाम्रो वेबसाइटमा तपाईंको विज्ञापन आकर्षक ब्यानरको रूपमा प्रदर्शित गरिन्छ।
✅ स्पोन्सर्ड लेख: तपाईंको व्यवसाय, सेवा, वा उत्पादनलाई विशेष समाचार वा लेखको रूपमा प्रकाशन गर्ने सुविधा।
✅ भिडियो विज्ञापन: हाम्रो डिजिटल प्लेटफर्ममा भिडियो विज्ञापन राखेर ठूलो दर्शकसम्म पुग्ने अवसर।
✅ सामाजिक सञ्जाल प्रवर्द्धन: फेसबुक, इन्स्टाग्राम, युट्युब जस्ता प्लेटफर्महरूमा तपाईंको विज्ञापनलाई प्रवर्द्धन गर्ने।

किन पोखरिया खबरमा विज्ञापन गर्ने?

🔹 स्थानीय पाठकहरूको ठूलो संख्या – हाम्रो वेबसाइटमा हजारौँ दर्शकहरू दैनिक आउँछन्।
🔹 सस्तो र प्रभावकारी विज्ञापन दर – अन्य मिडियाहरूभन्दा किफायती प्रचार विकल्पहरू।
🔹 टार्गेटेड मार्केटिङ – तपाईंको विज्ञापन सही दर्शकसम्म पुग्छ।
🔹 डिजिटल प्लेटफर्मको उच्च पहुँच – अनलाइन समाचार पोर्टल र सामाजिक सञ्जालहरू मार्फत ठूलो दर्शक समूह।

Entertain Lawyers (www.entertainlawyers.com) मा तपाईंको गोपनीयताको सम्मान र सुरक्षामा हाम्रो पूर्ण प्रतिबद्धता छ। यो गोपनीयता नीतिले हामीले तपाईंको जानकारी कसरी सङ्कलन, प्रयोग, र सुरक्षा गर्छौं भन्ने स्पष्ट पार्दछ।

१. हामीले सङ्कलन गर्ने जानकारी

हामी तपाईंबाट निम्न प्रकारका जानकारी सङ्कलन गर्न सक्छौं:

  • व्यक्तिगत जानकारी: तपाईंले हामीलाई सम्पर्क गर्दा वा सदस्यता लिँदा तपाईंको नाम, इमेल ठेगाना, र फोन नम्बर जस्ता विवरण माग्न सकिन्छ।

  • अव्यक्तिगत जानकारी: ब्राउजर प्रकार, यन्त्रको जानकारी, भ्रमण गरिएको पृष्ठहरू, र वेबसाइटमा बिताएको समय आदि ट्र्याक गर्न सकिन्छ ताकि हामी सेवा सुधार गर्न सकौं।

२. जानकारीको प्रयोग

हामी तपाईंको जानकारीलाई निम्न उद्देश्यका लागि प्रयोग गर्न सक्छौं:

  • तपाईंका जिज्ञासाको जवाफ दिन

  • अपडेट, समाचारपत्र, वा प्रचार सामग्री पठाउन (यदि तपाईंले सदस्यता लिनुभएको छ भने मात्र)

  • वेबसाइटको कार्यक्षमता सुधार गर्न

  • लक्षित विज्ञापन वा प्रायोजित सामग्री देखाउन

३. जानकारीको साझेदारी

हामी तपाईंको व्यक्तिगत जानकारीलाई तेस्रो पक्षसँग बेच्दैनौं वा साझा गर्दैनौं, बाहेक:

  • कानुनी बाध्यता पुरा गर्नुपर्ने अवस्थामा

  • वेबसाइट सञ्चालनमा सहयोग गर्ने सेवा प्रदायकहरूसँग (उनीहरूले गोपनीयता सम्झौता अन्तर्गत)

४. कुकीज (Cookies)

हाम्रो वेबसाइटले तपाईंको अनुभव सुधार गर्न र ट्राफिक विश्लेषण गर्न कुकीज प्रयोग गर्दछ। तपाईं आफ्नो ब्राउजर सेटिङमार्फत कुकी्स निष्क्रिय गर्न सक्नुहुन्छ।

५. डाटा सुरक्षा

हामी तपाईंको व्यक्तिगत जानकारी सुरक्षित राख्न उद्योग-स्तरीय उपायहरू अपनाउँछौं। यद्यपि, इन्टरनेट पूर्ण रूपमा सुरक्षित नभएकाले हामी पूर्ण सुरक्षा ग्यारेन्टी गर्न सक्दैनौं।

६. तेस्रो-पक्ष लिंकहरू

हाम्रो वेबसाइटमा बाह्य वेबसाइटहरूतर्फका लिङ्कहरू हुन सक्छन्। ती वेबसाइटहरूको गोपनीयता नीतिबारे हामी जिम्मेवार छैनौं।

७. बालबालिकाको गोपनीयता

हाम्रो वेबसाइट १३ वर्ष मुनिका बालबालिकाका लागि लक्षित गरिएको होइन। हामी त्यस्ता नाबालकहरूबाट जानाजानी जानकारी सङ्कलन गर्दैनौं।

८. नीतिमा परिवर्तन

हामी समय-समयमा यो गोपनीयता नीति अपडेट गर्न सक्छौं। कुनै पनि परिवर्तनहरू यसै पृष्ठमा प्रकाशित गरिनेछ।

९. हामीलाई सम्पर्क गर्नुहोस्

यदि तपाईंलाई यो गोपनीयता नीतिबारे कुनै जिज्ञासा छ भने हामीलाई सम्पर्क गर्नुहोस्:

📧 इमेल: contact@entertainlawyers.com
📱 फोन: +977-98XXXXXXXX

इंटरटेन लवयेर्स मा तपाईंको संस्था, सेवा वा उत्पादनको विज्ञापन प्रकाशन गर्न चाहनुहुन्छ?

हाम्रो पोर्टलमा कानूनप्रेमी, विद्यार्थी, अधिवक्ता, र सचेत पाठकहरूको पहुँच छ, जसले तपाईंको ब्राण्डलाई लक्षित समूहमा पुर्‍याउन मद्दत गर्दछ।

विज्ञापन राख्नका लागि तल दिइएको सम्पर्कमा सिधा सम्पर्क गर्नुहोस्:

📞 नाम: राम बाबु दास
🧑‍💼 पद: विज्ञापन व्यवस्थापक
📱 फोन नम्बर: +977-98XXXXXXXX

हामीसँग सम्पर्क गरेर आजै विज्ञापन बुक गर्नुहोस् र आफ्नो सन्देश हजारौं पाठकसम्म पुर्‍याउनुहोस्।

हामी तपाईंका सल्लाह, सुझाव, वा जिज्ञासाहरूको सदैव स्वागत गर्छौं। कानून र कानूनसँग सम्बन्धित सत्य र जानकारीमूलक सामग्री प्रकाशित गर्ने हाम्रो प्रयासमा तपाईंको सहभागिता र प्रतिक्रिया अमूल्य हुनेछ।

यदि तपाईं हामीसँग सम्पर्क गर्न चाहनुहुन्छ भने तलका विवरणहरू प्रयोग गर्नुहोस्:

🔹 फोन नम्बर: +977-98XXXXXXXX
🔹 इमेल: contact@entertainlawyers.com
🔹 वेबसाइट: www.entertainlawyers.com

सामान्य जानकारी, विज्ञापन सम्बन्धी सोधपुछ वा अन्य सहयोगका लागि हामीलाई सम्पर्क गर्नुहोस्।

हामी तपाईंको सन्देशको यथासक्य चाँडो जवाफ दिनेछौं।

इंटरटेन लवयेर्स नेपाली भाषामा प्रकाशित हुने एक अनलाइन न्युज पोर्टल हो, जसले कानून र कानूनसँग सम्बन्धित स्वच्छ, तथ्यपरक र जानकारीमूलक सामग्री प्रकाशन गर्छ। हामी विश्वसनीय समाचार र शिक्षाप्रद लेखहरूमार्फत नागरिकलाई कानुनी प्रणाली, यसको विकास, र अधिकारहरूबारे सचेत गराउने उद्देश्य राख्छौं।

हाम्रो उद्देश्य उत्तरदायी पत्रकारितालाई प्रवर्द्धन गर्नु र पाठकहरूका लागि कानुनी विषयमा भरपर्दो जानकारीको स्रोत बन्नु हो। अदालतको समाचार, कानुनी नीतिमा भएको परिवर्तन, वा कानूनप्रेमीहरूका लागि शिक्षामूलक सामग्री—हामी सधैं निष्पक्ष र स्पष्ट रिपोर्टिङमा विश्वास गर्छौं।

नेपालको कानुनी क्षेत्रलाई पारदर्शी बनाउने र जनतालाई सजिलो भाषामा कानुनी विषयबस्तु बुझाउन सहयोग पुर्‍याउनु नै हाम्रो प्रमुख लक्ष्य हो।

विश्वसनीय समाचार, महत्वपूर्ण छलफलहरू, र नेपालको कानून बुझ्नका लागि हामीसँग जोडिनुहोस्।

The Telugu film industry has delivered yet another powerful courtroom drama that is capturing the attention of audiences and sparking conversations: "Court: State vs. Nobody." Currently trending, this must-watch film delves into the sensitive and controversial issue of the misuse of the POCSO Act—a law intended to protect children from sexual offenses.

Set against the intense backdrop of a courtroom, the film explores how legal provisions designed to safeguard innocence can sometimes be manipulated, leading to life-altering consequences for the falsely accused. Through a tightly written narrative and compelling performances, "Court: State vs. Nobody" navigates the complex web of justice, truth, and redemption.

What truly stands out is the emotional depth and innocence of the characters, which resonates deeply with viewers. As the story unfolds, audiences find themselves engrossed in the battle between law and conscience, rooting for the truth to emerge victorious.

This film is more than just entertainment—it's a thought-provoking piece of cinema that raises awareness about the implications of legal loopholes. With its sharp writing, impactful courtroom sequences, and socially relevant message, "Court: State vs. Nobody" is undoubtedly a cinematic experience not to be missed.

12 Angry Men is a landmark in American cinema, renowned not only for its compelling narrative but also for its minimalist yet powerful setting—a single jury room. Directed by Sidney Lumet and released in 1957, the film is a gripping courtroom drama that explores the themes of justice, prejudice, and the strength of individual conviction.

The story follows twelve jurors who are tasked with deciding the fate of a teenage boy accused of murdering his father. At first glance, the case seems straightforward, and the majority of the jurors are ready to deliver a guilty verdict. However, the narrative takes a pivotal turn when Juror #8, portrayed by Henry Fonda, voices his doubts about the boy's guilt.

What follows is a tense, emotionally charged deliberation process. Juror #8 methodically questions the reliability of the evidence, urging the others to reconsider their initial judgments. As the discussion deepens, each juror’s personal biases, experiences, and character traits come to the fore, revealing the complex interplay between facts, assumptions, and the human psyche.

The film’s power lies in its simplicity—there are no dramatic flashbacks or courtroom theatrics. Instead, it relies on sharp dialogue, intense performances, and a gradually mounting sense of moral responsibility. Over time, the jurors confront their own prejudices and begin to see the case from new perspectives. What seemed like an open-and-shut decision evolves into a profound meditation on the meaning of justice.

With an IMDb rating of 9/10, 12 Angry Men continues to be celebrated as one of the greatest films ever made. It remains a staple in discussions about the American legal system and the ethical responsibilities of a jury. More than half a century after its release, its message about the importance of standing alone for what is right, even in the face of overwhelming opposition, still resonates powerfully.

In an age where quick judgments and snap decisions often dominate public discourse, 12 Angry Men serves as a timeless reminder of the need for patience, critical thinking, and empathy in the pursuit of justice.
post_title: 12 Angry Men: A Timeless Courtroom Drama Exploring Justice and Conviction

12 Angry Men is a landmark in American cinema, renowned not only for its compelling narrative but also for its minimalist yet powerful setting—a single jury room. Directed by Sidney Lumet and released in 1957, the film is a gripping courtroom drama that explores the themes of justice, prejudice, and the strength of individual conviction.

The story follows twelve jurors who are tasked with deciding the fate of a teenage boy accused of murdering his father. At first glance, the case seems straightforward, and the majority of the jurors are ready to deliver a guilty verdict. However, the narrative takes a pivotal turn when Juror #8, portrayed by Henry Fonda, voices his doubts about the boy's guilt.

What follows is a tense, emotionally charged deliberation process. Juror #8 methodically questions the reliability of the evidence, urging the others to reconsider their initial judgments. As the discussion deepens, each juror’s personal biases, experiences, and character traits come to the fore, revealing the complex interplay between facts, assumptions, and the human psyche.

The film’s power lies in its simplicity—there are no dramatic flashbacks or courtroom theatrics. Instead, it relies on sharp dialogue, intense performances, and a gradually mounting sense of moral responsibility. Over time, the jurors confront their own prejudices and begin to see the case from new perspectives. What seemed like an open-and-shut decision evolves into a profound meditation on the meaning of justice.

With an IMDb rating of 9/10, 12 Angry Men continues to be celebrated as one of the greatest films ever made. It remains a staple in discussions about the American legal system and the ethical responsibilities of a jury. More than half a century after its release, its message about the importance of standing alone for what is right, even in the face of overwhelming opposition, still resonates powerfully.

In an age where quick judgments and snap decisions often dominate public discourse, 12 Angry Men serves as a timeless reminder of the need for patience, critical thinking, and empathy in the pursuit of justice.

In an age where justice is often tangled in a web of politics, media noise, and public pressure, Jana Gana Mana emerges as a bold and thought-provoking film that challenges the very foundations of our legal and societal systems. Directed with sharp precision and powered by a compelling performance from Prithviraj Sukumaran, this 2022 legal thriller goes far beyond a typical crime drama—it becomes a reflection of the world we live in today.

The story begins with the brutal murder of a college lecturer, an incident that sends shockwaves through the community. As her body is burnt and the news spreads like wildfire, the public demands swift justice. Under pressure, the police force springs into action, led by a seemingly upright officer determined to bring the culprits to justice. But as the investigation unfolds, it becomes clear that the case is far from simple.

The narrative takes a gripping turn with the entrance of lawyer Aravind Swaminathan, portrayed powerfully by Prithviraj. Through intense courtroom scenes, Aravind dismantles the layers of the case with surgical precision—unearthing corruption, media manipulation, and deeply rooted political motives. His character not only drives the legal battle but also questions the very machinery meant to uphold justice.

What sets Jana Gana Mana apart is its unflinching critique of the legal system and the institutions surrounding it. The film doesn’t just stop at presenting a thrilling legal battle; it uses the courtroom as a platform to discuss larger issues like media trials, human rights, judicial integrity, and the misuse of public interest litigation. These themes resonate deeply in today’s socio-political climate, where the lines between justice and political theater often blur.

The movie also explores the power of sensationalized media in shaping public opinion and influencing the justice process. It questions how narratives are crafted, whose voices are amplified, and how the truth can be buried beneath noise and agendas.

Jana Gana Mana succeeds not only because of its engaging storyline but because of its ambition to start a conversation. It asks uncomfortable questions and refuses to offer easy answers. It invites the audience to reflect on how justice is served—and more importantly, who it serves.

In conclusion, Jana Gana Mana is more than just a film. It is a cinematic wake-up call that challenges viewers to think critically about the systems they trust. With its gripping narrative, stellar performances, and socially relevant themes, it stands as one of the most impactful Indian films in recent times.

Nepal's politics witnessed fresh turmoil as opposition parties demanded the resignation of Home Minister Ramesh Lekhak over a visit visa scandal. The controversy involved alleged misuse and irregularities in how visit visas were being issued.

Although there was no clear evidence proving Minister Lekhak’s direct involvement, the opposition argued that he should have stepped down to allow a fair and transparent investigation. They believed his position could have influenced the inquiry process.

His party, Nepali Congress, defended him, saying he was not involved in any wrongdoing and that the resignation calls were politically motivated.

Despite this, pressure from opposition parties continued to grow. Major groups like the CPN (Maoist Centre) and Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) warned they would block Tuesday’s parliamentary session if Lekhak did not resign.

A leader from the CPN (Maoist Centre) had stated, “We want accountability from those in power. The Home Minister should take responsibility.”

This situation created significant tension in the political arena. With both sides refusing to back down, the parliamentary session faced disruptions and strong debates. The country closely watched as the political drama unfolded.

Birgunj bench of the High Court has acquitted former Nepali Congress lawmaker Mohammad Aftab Alam in a high-profile murder case linked to a deadly bomb explosion and killing in Rautahat district.

Alam had earlier been convicted by the Rautahat District Court and sentenced to life imprisonment for his alleged role in the murder of a person by burning him alive in a brick kiln in Rajpur, Rautahat. The incident occurred on the night before the Constituent Assembly elections on 27 Chaitra 2064.

According to the District Court’s ruling, Alam was involved in detonating a bomb that injured several people. To hide evidence, it was alleged that he arranged for the injured individuals to be burned in a brick kiln. The case remained dormant for over a decade until Rautahat police arrested Alam on 19 Asoj 2076 — nearly 12 years after the incident.

The High Court, however, overturned the earlier verdict, citing lack of sufficient evidence to uphold the conviction. This acquittal has triggered varied responses across the political spectrum, with some calling for deeper scrutiny into the case, while others claim the court has rectified an unjust ruling.

Alam has consistently denied the charges, labeling them as politically motivated. The verdict brings a significant shift in one of the most talked-about criminal cases involving a political figure in recent Nepali history.
post_title: WAIT WHAT?? HIGH COURT ACQUITTED ALAM

Biranjan Yadav, 21, lived with his sister and brother-in-law in Ghattekulo, Kathmandu. A bright student, he was studying BBA on a scholarship at Saraswati Campus. However, his life changed drastically on Bhadra 23, 2076, when he was arrested by police from the Women’s Cell, Kalimati, in a rape case.
Despite being innocent, Biranjan spent 5 years and 8 months in prison. He was finally acquitted by a joint bench of Supreme Court Justices Til Prasad Shrestha and Bal Krishna Dhakal and released from Ramechhap Prison on Jestha 2, 2082.
A teenage girl, who lived below his flat and studied in grade 9, had accused him of rape. She claimed the incident took place on Shrawan 25, 2076, in Ghattekulo after meeting him in Maitidevi. She reported it to the police about a month later.
The case went through the Kathmandu District Court, Patan High Court, and the Supreme Court. The District Court sentenced him to 12 years, which was later reduced to 7 years by the High Court.
However, key facts were ignored: the girl had lied about her name and age. The court later found she was actually over 18 at the time. Her birth certificate and educational records did not match. The defense also argued the timeline of the incident was implausible.
Dr. Gajendra Aryal and Ram Ghimire, who defended Biranjan, argued the case was based on false information and poor investigation. Dr. Aryal even represented him for free due to the family's poor financial condition.
The Supreme Court acquitted Biranjan after confirming discrepancies in the victim’s documents. He now faces another battle — to be reinstated in his hometown, Birgunj, Ward No. 18 — as he tries to rebuild his life.
post_title: MAN ACQUITTED AFTER SPENDING 5 YEARS AND 8 MONTHS IN PRISON IN FALSE RAPE CASE

A complaint has been filed with the Judicial Council requesting an investigation and action against two High Court judges who acquitted former minister Mohammad Aftab Alam in the Rautahat bomb blast and murder case.
Yubaraj Poudel filed the complaint against Judges Dr. Khushi Prasad Tharu and Arjun Maharjan of the Birgunj bench at the Janakpur High Court. He alleges that the judges ignored the district court's verdict and the available evidence when they acquitted Alam. The complaint also calls for their immediate suspension, an investigation, and a review of their past rulings.

India's COVID-19 cases are rising again, with almost 3,000 active cases reported as of May 30. Just four days earlier, on May 26, there were only 1,010 cases. This shows a fast increase in infections.

Kerala has the highest number of cases at 1,147. After that, Maharashtra has 424 cases, Delhi has 294, and Gujarat has 223. Tamil Nadu and Karnataka both have 148 cases, while West Bengal has 116.

Other states with smaller numbers include Rajasthan (51), Uttar Pradesh (42), Puducherry (25), Haryana (20), Andhra Pradesh (16), Madhya Pradesh (10), Goa (7), and four each in Odisha, Punjab, and Jammu & Kashmir. Three cases each have been reported in Telangana, Arunachal Pradesh, and Chandigarh. Mizoram and Assam have two cases each.

No active cases have been found in Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, or the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Bihar’s data hasn’t been shared yet.

This month, at least seven people have died after testing positive for COVID-19. Two of them—one in Maharashtra and one in Delhi—had other serious health problems too. It’s still not clear if COVID-19 was the main cause of death for the others.

The flag of Nepal is unique over the world. It is only one flag in the world which in non-quadrilateral in shape. The flag of Nepal is consisting of two triangular shapes. It has a crimson background with a dark blue border. The upper segment has a white moon emitting eight rays, with a crescent attached below. A white, stylized sun with 12 rays is in the flag's bottom section. BUT WHO DESIGNED? The flag of Nepal is designed by 89 years engineer and architect Shankar Nath Rimal. He was designed the flag on the request of King Mahendra about in 2018 BS(about 62 years ago). Rimal remembered, when king Mahendra asked him 'can you do it?, He replied 'yes, I can do it'. THIS INCIDENT CALLED HIM !! According to Rimal, after Nepal became a member of the United Nations, one flag was used when the minister went, another flag was used when the king went, and another flag was used when the secretary went. After seeing different flags, Nepal was asked, which is the official flag of Nepal? Everyone was shocked. This news reached the king. And then king Mahendra during the time of formation of New constitution in 2018, he called Rimal to design the flag.
FLAG WAS NOT ALWAYS LIKE THIS!! Before 2019, there was no standard flag in Nepal. It was customary to keep two triangles and moon and sun since tradition. Some used to put the sun above and some below to make the flag. Human faces were also placed on it. "The moon and the sun means, whatever you imagine, but the triangle, the moon and the sun, red and blue colors are what anyone would have."
HIS REMARKABLE WORKS!! He designed the attractive Shaheed Gate of the capital Kathmandu, which was inaugurated by King Mahendra on 1st Baisakh of the year 2018. Hotel Solti, Nepal Pragya-Pratishthan, Amrit Science College, Shantigriha, Sharada Sadan, Bhairahawa and Pokhara Nepal Rashtra Bank and Ramanada Chowk Janakpur Entrance gate.
HIS BACKGROUND? Rimal was Born in Tangal, Kathmandu, and he passed engineering in 1957 from Bengal Engineering College under Kolkata University. After that he was employed at Sadar Public Niksari Adda. He was also the Secretary General of Nepal Art council.

A private university in Beijing has sparked outrage after a disturbing incident involving a female student. She claimed that staff at the campus clinic asked her to pull down her pants to prove she was menstruating in order to get sick leave.

The incident happened at the Gengdan Institute of Beijing University of Technology, an independent college linked to one of China’s top public universities. On May 15, the student posted a video online describing what happened. The video quickly went viral on Chinese social media.

In the video, the student is heard confronting a female staff member at the clinic, asking why such an invasive request was necessary.

“So, you're saying every woman on her period has to take off her pants and show you to get a leave note?” the student asks.

“Basically, yes. It’s not my personal rule, it’s a regulation,” the staff member replies.

When the student asks to see the regulation in writing, the staff member goes silent but continues to refuse the leave note. She tells the student to go to a hospital for proof instead.

CPN (Maoist Center) Chairman Pushpa Kamal Dahal Prachanda has said that bricks thrown by monarchists should be answered with stones.

Speaking at the Third National Conference of the Young Communist League on Sunday, Prachanda stated, “We want to live peacefully, but if we are attacked, we will respond with stones to their bricks.”

He added, “We won’t start any violence ourselves. We’ll tell the people that our movement is peaceful. But if anyone tries to attack us, we will defend ourselves. We are ready. If needed, we can even lead another rebellion.”

Prachanda explained that their ongoing campaign is a preparation for a possible future socialist revolution. “There can be no revolution without connecting with the people. What we are doing now is getting ready for that,” he said.

He also emphasized that it is the responsibility of the Maoist Center to protect the republic.

post_content: After the temporary bench of the High Court Janakpur in Birgunj said there was no proof that the victims were burned alive, people started asking what really happened to them. Shri Narayan Singh, the 84-year-old father of Trilok Pratap, asked, "If no one burned them in a brick kiln after putting them in sacks, then where is my son Trilok Pratap?"   [caption id="attachment_2454" align="alignnone" width="300"] Deceased Trilok Pratap's Father[/caption] He didn’t accept the High Court’s decision and demanded answers. “If the court can’t confirm my son was killed, then the government must find him,” he said. Even at 84, he promised to keep fighting for justice. “What more proof do you need? Where is my son? The government must find out. Whether he’s alive or dead, they must tell us. We are just ordinary people,” he added. [caption id="attachment_2428" align="alignnone" width="300"] Judges who acquitted Aftab Alam[/caption] Trilok was 22 when he died. He was Shri Narayan’s youngest son and studied Political Science at Goenka College in Sitamarhi, India. Shri Narayan, a strong supporter of the Nepali Congress, had sent his son to help with an election campaign at the request of Mohammad Aftab Alam. While still in college, Trilok worked hard on the campaign—writing speeches and handling publicity. “I was born in a country where politicians think they are above the law,” his father said. “A judge should stand for justice.”
post_title: TRILOK PRATAP'S FATHER'S QUESTION: IF MY SON WASN'T KILLED, WHERE IS HE?

A royalist group has announced a shutdown in the Kathmandu Valley on Monday, after the arrest of RPP Nepal Chairman Kamal Thapa and RPP Member of Parliament Deepak Singh.

The Joint People's Movement Committee, led by Nawaraj Subedi, released a statement on Sunday, saying that the police arrested Thapa, Singh, and others in a harsh and unfair way during a peaceful protest.

The committee has demanded that the government immediately release everyone who was arrested.

They also said the protest movement will now take a different form, and they have called for a Valley-wide shutdown on Monday (Jestha 19).

In the statement, Subedi asked supporters to actively participate in the protest by gathering in their own neighborhoods and local squares.

Leaders and activists of the RPP Nepal, including Chairman Thapa, were arrested after a royalist group protested from the Narayan Chaur area of the capital on Sunday and tried to enter Baluwatar.

post_content: After the Birgunj bench of judges Khushi Prasad Tharu and Arjun Maharjan overturned the life sentence imposed by the Rautahat District Court, questions have been raised about the judiciary itself. The bench of Tharu and Maharjan acquitted the accused, stating that there was no solid evidence to support the claim that a bomb exploded in Alam's house on Chaitra 28, 2064, and that those injured in the explosion were loaded onto a tractor and thrown into a brick kiln to be burned. Fifteen eyewitnesses to the incident appeared before the court and testified. Following the acquittal of the culprits in such a heinous crime, the competence of the judges has been questioned. Yubaraj Poudel filed a complaint with the Judicial Council on Friday, demanding an investigation into the High Court's decision regarding Alam and action against the judges. Among the judges who made the decision, Tharu was appointed as a High Court judge from the Congress quota in 2073 BS. Tharu is also one of the 80 controversially appointed judges, known as the 'Midnight Judges.' When Sushila Karki was the chairperson of the Judicial Council, the law minister was Ajay Shankar Nayak of the Maoists. Although he was a minister, the ones who obstructed the appointment of judges were Ramesh Lekhak from the Congress and Barshaman Pun from the Maoists. Karki has publicly stated that the Ramesh Lekhak appointed other judges, including Tharu, from his party quota after a dispute with her. The same judge Tharu had acquitted Vijay Kumar Gachhadar and others in the Baluwatar case in 2080 Falgun when he was in special court. Another judge, Maharjan, who acquitted Alam, was appointed as a High Court judge from the Maoist quota on Bhadra 29, 2080. At that time, the council had recommended 27 judges for appointment to the High Court out of 56 vacancies, of which only six were from legal practitioners. Council Chairman and Chief Justice Bishwambhar Shrestha had appointed 27 people as judges of the High Court amid controversy after a prolonged vacancy. Maharjan, who worked in the firm of former Nepal Bar President Chandeshwor Shrestha, became a judge from the quota of the Maoists, led by the then-government. According to sources, the then-Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister Narayan Kaji Shrestha played a decisive role in his appointment as a judge. At that time, Prachanda was the Prime Minister under the Congress-Maoist alliance, and Dhanraj Gurung was the Law Minister.
post_title: PRACHNADA'S QUESTION TO NARAYAN KAJI: WHY DID YOU WRITE ON FACEBOOK AGAINST A JUDGE APPOINTED ON YOUR OWN RECOMMENDATION?

May 31, 2025, in West Bengal's South 24 Parganas district, specifically in the Bharatgarh area of Basanti. The man, identified as Bimal Mondal, was arrested after he was seen walking through the streets carrying the severed head of his sister-in-law, named Sati Mondal or Pratima Mondal in different reports, along with a chopper or sickle-like weapon used in the crime.

The murder stemmed from a family dispute, possibly related to property issues or longstanding tensions, which escalated into a violent altercation. Locals alerted the police after witnessing the gruesome scene, and some recorded videos of Bimal walking with the severed head. He reportedly walked nearly three miles toward the Basanti police station, where he surrendered, still carrying the head and the weapon.

The victim's body was found in a field, and the police have sent it for post-mortem examination while seizing the murder weapon. Initial investigations suggest the crime occurred late Friday night or early Saturday morning, with a forensic team now examining the scene.

Eyewitnesses noted Bimal's intense rage, as he was heard cursing the victim and her husband, claiming he was avenging years of perceived injustice. The local community is in shock, as frequent quarrels between Bimal and the victim had been reported, but no one anticipated such a horrific act.

Locals alerted the police after witnessing the gruesome scene, and some recorded videos of Bimal walking with the severed head. He reportedly walked nearly three miles toward the Basanti police station, where he surrendered, still carrying the head and the weapon.

The victim's body was found in a field, and the police have sent it for post-mortem examination while seizing the murder weapon. Initial investigations suggest the crime occurred late Friday night or early Saturday morning, with a forensic team now examining the scene.

Eyewitnesses noted Bimal's intense rage, as he was heard cursing the victim and her husband, claiming he was avenging years of perceived injustice. The local community is in shock, as frequent quarrels between Bimal and the victim had been reported, but no one anticipated such a horrific act.

Justice Sapana Pradhan Malla has been serving as a Justice of the Supreme Court of Nepal since 2073 B.S. (2016 A.D.). She was born on November 15, 1963 A.D.(2020 Karthik 29 B.S.), in Nawalparasi district. She obtained her Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) from Tribhuvan University in 1987(2044 B.S.) and went on to pursue a Master’s in Comparative Law from Delhi University in 1989(2046 B.S.). Additionally, she holds a degree in Political Science and earned a Mid-Career Master in Public Administration from Harvard University in 2014(2071 B.S.). Justice Malla is currently one of only two female justices appointed to the Supreme Court of Nepal. Prior to her judicial appointment, she served as a member of the Constituent Assembly from 2065 to 2069 B.S. (2008–2013 A.D.). She is notably recognized for her role as an advocate in the landmark Godavari Marble Case. Throughout her career, Justice Malla has been a steadfast advocate for women's empowerment, gender equality, and human rights. She served as a member of the United Nations Committee against Torture (CAT) from 2014 to 2017 and is the former President of the Forum for Women, Law and Development (FWLD). Her contributions to the advancement of women's rights have earned her significant recognition, including the prestigious Gruber International Women’s Rights Award (2008) from the Peter and Patricia Gruber Foundation (USA), and the Prashiddha Prabal Jansewashree, Second Class award conferred by the Government of Nepal in 2078 B.S. Justice Malla has also contributed extensively to legal and academic discourse through her writings. Her notable publications include:
  • “Women Empowerment”, The Kathmandu Post, May 5, 2004
  • “Violation of Human Rights of Women”, The Rising Nepal, July 13, 1990
  • “Sex Equality—Approaches and Judicial Intervention”, Supreme Court 50th Anniversary Special Volume, p. 190, 2006
  • “Women’s Access to Justice”, Annapurna Post, Shrawan 1, 2068 (2011)
  • “Violence Against Women and Law”, Nyayadoot, Year 29, No. 106, Vol. 4, 1998, p. 45
In addition, she conducted a pivotal study titled “Women’s Participation in the Political Process of Nepal”, published by the Asia Pacific Forum on Women, Law and Development (APWLD) in 1999. Currently, Justice Malla is regarded as a leading candidate for appointment as the next Chief Justice of Nepal, which would make her the second woman in the nation's history to hold that esteemed position.
post_title: KNOW ABOUT HONORABLE JUSTICE SAPANA PRADHAN MALLA

A writ petition has been filed in the Supreme Court against the public transport strike called by the National Federation of Nepal Transport Entrepreneurs. On Tuesday, advocate Bivek Pokharel filed the petition, naming the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Physical Infrastructure and Transport, and the Federation as defendants.

The petition is scheduled for hearing on Wednesday. It seeks an interim order to immediately resume public transport services, arguing that the strike violates the Constitution. Public transport is classified as an essential service, and strikes in such sectors are prohibited by law.

The petition claims that the strike has violated the fundamental rights of citizens by restricting their freedom of movement, profession, and employment rights that are guaranteed under Article 17, Sub article 2 of the Constitution.

An emergency meeting of the Judicial Council is scheduled to be held to initiate the investigation process against the judges who acquitted Nepali Congress MP Mohammad Aftab Alam in a murder case.

Judicial Council Chairman and Chief Justice Prakash Man Singh Raut has directed that an emergency meeting be convened at 9 AM on Wednesday. "The agenda of the meeting will include the appointment of judges and other matters, but the primary focus will be the decision to acquit Alam," a Judicial Council source said. "Today's meeting is likely to concentrate on this issue."

A few days ago, during an informal "zero hour" meeting of the Supreme Court judges, this issue was raised loudly and seriously. After questions began to arise from all sides, the Chief Justice, in consultation with the council members, fixed the date for the meeting.

The Judicial Council, led by Chief Justice Prakash Man Singh Raut, includes the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court, Sapana Pradhan Malla; members Ram Prasad Bhandari and Damodar Khadka; and Law Minister Ajay Kumar Chaurasia.

The Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court has issued a mandamus order against former Speaker Agni Sapkota in connection with a murder case.

With this order, the path has now opened for investigation and prosecution of Sapkota in the case of the abduction and subsequent murder of Arjun Lama from Kavre.

According to the Supreme Court's website, the order was issued on Wednesday by a Constitutional Bench comprising Chief Justice Prakashman Singh Raut, along with Justices Sapana Pradhan Malla, Kumar Regmi, Manoj Kumar Sharma, and Kumar Chudal.

A writ petition had been filed by journalist Kanak Mani Dixit, Arjun Lama’s wife Purnimaya Lama, and human rights activist Sushil Pyakurel, demanding justice and punishment for Sapkota, accusing him of involvement in Lama’s abduction and murder in Kavre.

Purnimaya Lama had initially filed the case against Sapkota in 2069 BS (2012 AD), alleging his involvement in the murder of her husband. At the time the case was filed, Sapkota had been appointed Minister of Information and Communications.

Arjun Lama had been abducted and killed in Kavre in 2062 BS (2005 AD). Sapkota has consistently denied the allegations, arguing that the case should be treated as a conflict-era incident and therefore not subject to regular criminal prosecution.
post_title: MURDER CASE AGAINST EX SPEAKER REVIVED

Purnimaya Lama had initially filed the case against Sapkota in 2069 BS (2012 AD), alleging his involvement in the murder of her husband. At the time the case was filed, Sapkota had been appointed Minister of Information and Communications.

Arjun Lama had been abducted and killed in Kavre in 2062 BS (2005 AD). Sapkota has consistently denied the allegations, arguing that the case should be treated as a conflict-era incident and therefore not subject to regular criminal prosecution.

A corruption case has been filed against former Prime Minister of Nepal Madhav Kumar Nepal, the chairman of the CPN (Unified Socialist Party). Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority(CIAA) filed the corruption case against Nepal related to the Patanjali land embezzlement case in the special court where claim(bigo) of 18 crore 15 lakhs and 50 thousand has been made.

Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority had taken a statement from Madhav Kumar Nepal, alleging that he had bought and sold land in the name of Patanjali Yoga Peeth and Ayurvedic Company in Kavre, which was exempt from the limit.

In 2066 BS, when Madhav Kumar Nepal was the Prime Minister, the Council of Ministers approved the purchase of land exempt from the limit. However, after a complaint was received that land was being sold illegally in excess of the limit, the CIAA initiated an investigation into the matter. CIAA has filed a case against 93 people, including Madhav Kumar Nepal. The case has been filed in the special court against former Law Minister Prem Bahadur Singh, then Land Reforms Secretary Chhabi Raj Pant, and others. With the registration of this case, MP Madhav Kumar Nepal has been suspended from his post.
post_title: Corruption case against Madhav Kumar Nepal

post_content: Four members of a Nepali family were found dead inside their apartment in Manassas Park, Virginia, on Thursday night. The victims include a 38-year-old man, a 36-year-old woman, their 8-year-old daughter, and 2-year-old son. Police said all four died from gunshot wounds. A gun was found at the scene. The family members have been identified as Santosh Pariyar, Anju Shrestha, and their two children. The police were called to the apartment around 10:40 PM after the landlord became worried. The landlord said he had not heard from the family for several days. When police entered the home, they found all four people dead. Officers say the case may be a murder-suicide, but they have not confirmed who fired the gun. The bodies have been sent for post-mortem examination, and the investigation is still ongoing. Neighbors told police that the family had moved to the U.S. from Nepal about six months ago. The Nepali community in the area is deeply saddened by the incident.
post_title: Four Nepali Family Members Found Dead in Virginia, USA

post_content:
I. Introduction: Why Protest Matters In any functioning democracy, the right to protest isn’t just a legal footnote — it’s the heartbeat of civic life. It’s how everyday people, often with little power or privilege, make their voices heard. Whether it’s marching for justice, speaking out against inequality, or standing up to government overreach, protest has always been a powerful driver of change. History offers countless examples: from the Civil Rights Movement in the U.S. to India’s independence struggle and today’s global climate strikes. These weren’t polite conversations — they were often loud, disruptive, and uncomfortable. And yet, they moved societies forward. But across the world today — and right here in Nepal — this right is increasingly under pressure. Governments, citing “national security” or “public order,” are making it harder and riskier for people to speak up. While some rules are necessary to maintain peace, many are being used as tools of control rather than protection. This article explores the evolving landscape of protest rights, looking closely at international standards and how they’re being applied — or misused — in Nepal. The deeper question it asks is this: Are we watching a slow erosion of democracy in real time? II. What Is Protest — And Why Does It Matter? At its core, protest is a form of communication. It’s people saying, “We see injustice, and we won’t stay silent.” Protests can look different — marches, sit-ins, strikes, online campaigns, even peaceful disobedience — but their essence is the same: public expression of collective dissent. This right isn’t just a standalone concept. It’s deeply connected to three fundamental freedoms:
  • Freedom of expression
  • Freedom of peaceful assembly
  • Freedom of association
Importantly, protests don’t have to be polite or convenient to be legitimate. They only need to be peaceful — meaning no incitement to violence or imminent threat to public safety. Even disruptive or loud protests can be protected under the law. In many ways, protest serves as a democratic pressure valve — a way for the public to hold power to account, share frustrations, and demand change when other systems fail. III. What International Law Says About the Right to Protest Across international human rights law, the right to protest is widely recognized — not as a privilege, but as a basic entitlement:
  1. Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948)
  • Article 20(1): “Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association.” Though not binding, this document set the moral foundation for modern human rights protections.
  1. International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR, 1966)
  • Article 21: Protects peaceful assembly. Restrictions must be lawful, necessary, and proportionate — not just convenient for governments. Nepal is a signatory, meaning it has legally committed to uphold this right.
  1. UN Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 37 (2020)
  • Asserts that governments not only must not interfere with peaceful protest — they must actively facilitate it.
  • Public spaces are for the public. Restricting protest is the exception, not the rule.
  1. Regional Human Rights Protections
  • European, American, and African human rights conventions all protect peaceful assembly — reinforcing its global significance.
IV.  Around the World: How Protest Is Being Suppressed
  1. Using Laws to Silence Dissent
     United Kingdom
  • The Public Order Act 2023 introduced the vague term “serious disruption,” giving the state broad power to restrict protests.
  • Climate activists have been imprisoned for simply walking slowly — deemed disruptive.
     Australia
  • Over 36 new anti-protest laws have been introduced, mostly targeting environmental activism.
  • Penalties include heavy fines and imprisonment, raising concerns about corporate influence over free speech.
     France & Germany
  • Blanket bans on certain protests — especially those in support of Palestine — have raised alarms over discriminatory double standards.
  1. Force, Fear, and Surveillance
  • In the U.S., Belarus, Hong Kong, and beyond, protesters have faced rubber bullets, water cannons, and arbitrary arrests.
  • Governments are also deploying facial recognition, phone tracking, and online surveillance to identify and intimidate protest leaders.
  1. The Chilling Effect
  • Vaguely written laws make it easy for authorities to label peaceful dissent as criminal.
  • Protesters are often smeared as “troublemakers” or “threats,” discouraging civic participation and weakening public trust in democratic institutions.
V.  Nepal: Constitutional Promises, On-the-Ground Reality
  1. What the Constitution Says
Nepal’s 2015 Constitution, a landmark democratic document, guarantees the right to protest:
  • Article 17(2)(b): Right to assemble peacefully and without arms
  • Article 17(2)(a): Freedom of opinion and expression
On paper, this aligns with international standards. In practice, things look very different.
  1. The Laws That Govern Protests
  • Civil Rights Act, 1955: Protects speech and assembly
  • Local Administration Act, 1971: Gives Chief District Officers (CDOs) broad powers to ban or restrict protests — often with little oversight
  1. Courts Speak — But Are They Heard?
  • Maitighar Mandala Case (2018): Supreme Court upheld protest rights at a traditional protest site. But enforcement has been inconsistent.
  • Giri Bandobast Case: The Court emphasized that preventive detention shouldn’t be used to shut down peaceful protest — but executive overreach continues.
  1. Real Stories of Suppression
  • In September 2024, activist Ruby Khan and others were arrested while protesting unlawful land grabs. Their protest was peaceful, but they were accused of disturbing public order.
  • The Terai Human Rights Defenders Alliance reports that 37 people — mostly from marginalized communities — have died in protest-related incidents over the last decade.
  1. A Region-Wide Problem
Nepal is not alone. India’s Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code, for instance, is often used to restrict assemblies with little justification. Both countries share a worrying trend: the routine overuse of legal tools to shrink democratic space. VI. When Can Governments Legally Limit Protests? Under international law, restrictions are allowed, but only under strict conditions:
  • Legality: The rule must be clear and written into law
  • Legitimacy: The goal must be legitimate — like protecting safety, not silencing criticism
  • Necessity & Proportionality: The restriction must be absolutely necessary and not go further than needed
Vague bans, sweeping arrests, and criminalizing speech often fail all three tests. VI- A. The New Frontline: Digital Protests As more protests move online, governments are adapting — not by listening, but by cracking down digitally. In Nepal, the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 is increasingly used to charge social media users who criticize the government — even when the speech is peaceful and non-defamatory. Globally, digital dissent is under threat too. Internet shutdowns, social media censorship, and algorithmic filtering are becoming modern forms of protest suppression. It’s time we recognized digital protest as an extension of the right to peaceful assembly. VII. What Needs to Change: Reform and Resistance
  1. Reform the Law
  • Amend the Local Administration Act to limit unchecked CDO powers
  • Revise vague or overly broad laws like the Electronic Transactions Act
  • Decriminalize peaceful protest once and for all
  1. Train and Watch the Police
  • Require human rights training for law enforcement
  • Create independent bodies to investigate police violence and misconduct during protests
  1. Protect the Digital Space
  • Enshrine the right to online speech and protest in national law
  • Ensure cybercrime laws aren’t weaponized against activists and journalists
  1. Strengthen Civil Society
  • Support groups that document abuse, provide legal aid, and train citizens on their rights
  • Encourage media to cover protests fairly and avoid harmful stereotypes
VIII. Conclusion: Reclaiming Democratic Space The right to protest is not chaos — it’s democracy in motion. Its how change begins, how governments are held to account, and how people turn pain into purpose. In Nepal and around the world, this right is under siege. But the solution isn’t silence. It’s solidarity. Legal reforms are critical, yes — but so is civic courage. Judges, journalists, lawyers, students, and citizens must all step up. Because the real threat to public order isn’t protest. It’s the erosion of the freedom to protest at all.
post_title: The Right to Protest: Legal Limits and Government Crackdowns – A Global and Nepali Perspective

  1. UN Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 37 (2020)
  • Asserts that governments not only must not interfere with peaceful protest — they must actively facilitate it.
  • Public spaces are for the public. Restricting protest is the exception, not the rule.
  1. Regional Human Rights Protections
  • European, American, and African human rights conventions all protect peaceful assembly — reinforcing its global significance.
IV.  Around the World: How Protest Is Being Suppressed
  1. Using Laws to Silence Dissent
     United Kingdom
  • The Public Order Act 2023 introduced the vague term “serious disruption,” giving the state broad power to restrict protests.
  • Climate activists have been imprisoned for simply walking slowly — deemed disruptive.
     Australia
  • Over 36 new anti-protest laws have been introduced, mostly targeting environmental activism.
  • Penalties include heavy fines and imprisonment, raising concerns about corporate influence over free speech.
     France & Germany
  • Blanket bans on certain protests — especially those in support of Palestine — have raised alarms over discriminatory double standards.
  1. Force, Fear, and Surveillance
  • In the U.S., Belarus, Hong Kong, and beyond, protesters have faced rubber bullets, water cannons, and arbitrary arrests.
  • Governments are also deploying facial recognition, phone tracking, and online surveillance to identify and intimidate protest leaders.
  1. The Chilling Effect
  • Vaguely written laws make it easy for authorities to label peaceful dissent as criminal.
  • Protesters are often smeared as “troublemakers” or “threats,” discouraging civic participation and weakening public trust in democratic institutions.
V.  Nepal: Constitutional Promises, On-the-Ground Reality
  1. What the Constitution Says
Nepal’s 2015 Constitution, a landmark democratic document, guarantees the right to protest:
  • Article 17(2)(b): Right to assemble peacefully and without arms
  • Article 17(2)(a): Freedom of opinion and expression
On paper, this aligns with international standards. In practice, things look very different.
  1. The Laws That Govern Protests
  • Civil Rights Act, 1955: Protects speech and assembly
  • Local Administration Act, 1971: Gives Chief District Officers (CDOs) broad powers to ban or restrict protests — often with little oversight
  1. Courts Speak — But Are They Heard?
  • Maitighar Mandala Case (2018): Supreme Court upheld protest rights at a traditional protest site. But enforcement has been inconsistent.
  • Giri Bandobast Case: The Court emphasized that preventive detention shouldn’t be used to shut down peaceful protest — but executive overreach continues.
  1. Real Stories of Suppression
  • In September 2024, activist Ruby Khan and others were arrested while protesting unlawful land grabs. Their protest was peaceful, but they were accused of disturbing public order.
  • The Terai Human Rights Defenders Alliance reports that 37 people — mostly from marginalized communities — have died in protest-related incidents over the last decade.
  1. A Region-Wide Problem
Nepal is not alone. India’s Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code, for instance, is often used to restrict assemblies with little justification. Both countries share a worrying trend: the routine overuse of legal tools to shrink democratic space. VI. When Can Governments Legally Limit Protests? Under international law, restrictions are allowed, but only under strict conditions:
  • Legality: The rule must be clear and written into law
  • Legitimacy: The goal must be legitimate — like protecting safety, not silencing criticism
  • Necessity & Proportionality: The restriction must be absolutely necessary and not go further than needed
Vague bans, sweeping arrests, and criminalizing speech often fail all three tests. VI- A. The New Frontline: Digital Protests As more protests move online, governments are adapting — not by listening, but by cracking down digitally. In Nepal, the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 is increasingly used to charge social media users who criticize the government — even when the speech is peaceful and non-defamatory. Globally, digital dissent is under threat too. Internet shutdowns, social media censorship, and algorithmic filtering are becoming modern forms of protest suppression. It’s time we recognized digital protest as an extension of the right to peaceful assembly. VII. What Needs to Change: Reform and Resistance
  1. Reform the Law
  • Amend the Local Administration Act to limit unchecked CDO powers
  • Revise vague or overly broad laws like the Electronic Transactions Act
  • Decriminalize peaceful protest once and for all
  1. Train and Watch the Police
  • Require human rights training for law enforcement
  • Create independent bodies to investigate police violence and misconduct during protests
  1. Protect the Digital Space
  • Enshrine the right to online speech and protest in national law
  • Ensure cybercrime laws aren’t weaponized against activists and journalists
  1. Strengthen Civil Society
  • Support groups that document abuse, provide legal aid, and train citizens on their rights
  • Encourage media to cover protests fairly and avoid harmful stereotypes
VIII. Conclusion: Reclaiming Democratic Space The right to protest is not chaos — it’s democracy in motion. Its how change begins, how governments are held to account, and how people turn pain into purpose. In Nepal and around the world, this right is under siege. But the solution isn’t silence. It’s solidarity. Legal reforms are critical, yes — but so is civic courage. Judges, journalists, lawyers, students, and citizens must all step up. Because the real threat to public order isn’t protest. It’s the erosion of the freedom to protest at all.

These weren’t polite conversations — they were often loud, disruptive, and uncomfortable. And yet, they moved societies forward. But across the world today — and right here in Nepal — this right is increasingly under pressure. Governments, citing “national security” or “public order,” are making it harder and riskier for people to speak up. While some rules are necessary to maintain peace, many are being used as tools of control rather than protection. This article explores the evolving landscape of protest rights, looking closely at international standards and how they’re being applied — or misused — in Nepal. The deeper question it asks is this: Are we watching a slow erosion of democracy in real time? II. What Is Protest — And Why Does It Matter? At its core, protest is a form of communication. It’s people saying, “We see injustice, and we won’t stay silent.” Protests can look different — marches, sit-ins, strikes, online campaigns, even peaceful disobedience — but their essence is the same: public expression of collective dissent. This right isn’t just a standalone concept. It’s deeply connected to three fundamental freedoms:
  • Freedom of expression
  • Freedom of peaceful assembly
  • Freedom of association
Importantly, protests don’t have to be polite or convenient to be legitimate. They only need to be peaceful — meaning no incitement to violence or imminent threat to public safety. Even disruptive or loud protests can be protected under the law. In many ways, protest serves as a democratic pressure valve — a way for the public to hold power to account, share frustrations, and demand change when other systems fail. III. What International Law Says About the Right to Protest Across international human rights law, the right to protest is widely recognized — not as a privilege, but as a basic entitlement:
    1. Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948)
    1. Article 20(1): “Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association.” Though not binding, this document set the moral foundation for modern human rights protections.
      1. International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR, 1966)
      • Article 21: Protects peaceful assembly. Restrictions must be lawful, necessary, and proportionate — not just convenient for governments. Nepal is a signatory, meaning it has legally committed to uphold this right.
      1. UN Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 37 (2020)
      • Asserts that governments not only must not interfere with peaceful protest — they must actively facilitate it.
      • Public spaces are for the public. Restricting protest is the exception, not the rule.
      1. Regional Human Rights Protections
      • European, American, and African human rights conventions all protect peaceful assembly — reinforcing its global significance.
IV.  Around the World: How Protest Is Being Suppressed
      1. Using Laws to Silence Dissent
     United Kingdom
      • The Public Order Act 2023 introduced the vague term “serious disruption,” giving the state broad power to restrict protests.
      • Climate activists have been imprisoned for simply walking slowly — deemed disruptive.
     Australia
      • Over 36 new anti-protest laws have been introduced, mostly targeting environmental activism.
      • Penalties include heavy fines and imprisonment, raising concerns about corporate influence over free speech.
     France & Germany
      • Blanket bans on certain protests — especially those in support of Palestine — have raised alarms over discriminatory double standards.
      1. Force, Fear, and Surveillance
      • In the U.S., Belarus, Hong Kong, and beyond, protesters have faced rubber bullets, water cannons, and arbitrary arrests.
      • Governments are also deploying facial recognition, phone tracking, and online surveillance to identify and intimidate protest leaders.
      1. The Chilling Effect
      • Vaguely written laws make it easy for authorities to label peaceful dissent as criminal.
      • Protesters are often smeared as “troublemakers” or “threats,” discouraging civic participation and weakening public trust in democratic institutions.
V.  Nepal: Constitutional Promises, On-the-Ground Reality
      1. What the Constitution Says
Nepal’s 2015 Constitution, a landmark democratic document, guarantees the right to protest:
      • Article 17(2)(b): Right to assemble peacefully and without arms
      • Article 17(2)(a): Freedom of opinion and expression
On paper, this aligns with international standards. In practice, things look very different.
      1. The Laws That Govern Protests
      • Civil Rights Act, 1955: Protects speech and assembly
      • Local Administration Act, 1971: Gives Chief District Officers (CDOs) broad powers to ban or restrict protests — often with little oversight
      1. Courts Speak — But Are They Heard?
      • Maitighar Mandala Case (2018): Supreme Court upheld protest rights at a traditional protest site. But enforcement has been inconsistent.
      • Giri Bandobast Case: The Court emphasized that preventive detention shouldn’t be used to shut down peaceful protest — but executive overreach continues.
      1. Real Stories of Suppression
      • In September 2024, activist Ruby Khan and others were arrested while protesting unlawful land grabs. Their protest was peaceful, but they were accused of disturbing public order.
      • The Terai Human Rights Defenders Alliance reports that 37 people — mostly from marginalized communities — have died in protest-related incidents over the last decade.
      1. A Region-Wide Problem
Nepal is not alone. India’s Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code, for instance, is often used to restrict assemblies with little justification. Both countries share a worrying trend: the routine overuse of legal tools to shrink democratic space. VI. When Can Governments Legally Limit Protests? Under international law, restrictions are allowed, but only under strict conditions:
      • Legality: The rule must be clear and written into law
      • Legitimacy: The goal must be legitimate — like protecting safety, not silencing criticism
      • Necessity & Proportionality: The restriction must be absolutely necessary and not go further than needed
Vague bans, sweeping arrests, and criminalizing speech often fail all three tests. VI- A. The New Frontline: Digital Protests As more protests move online, governments are adapting — not by listening, but by cracking down digitally. In Nepal, the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 is increasingly used to charge social media users who criticize the government — even when the speech is peaceful and non-defamatory. Globally, digital dissent is under threat too. Internet shutdowns, social media censorship, and algorithmic filtering are becoming modern forms of protest suppression. It’s time we recognized digital protest as an extension of the right to peaceful assembly. VII. What Needs to Change: Reform and Resistance
      1. Reform the Law
      • Amend the Local Administration Act to limit unchecked CDO powers
      • Revise vague or overly broad laws like the Electronic Transactions Act
      • Decriminalize peaceful protest once and for all
      1. Train and Watch the Police
      • Require human rights training for law enforcement
      • Create independent bodies to investigate police violence and misconduct during protests
      1. Protect the Digital Space
      • Enshrine the right to online speech and protest in national law
      • Ensure cybercrime laws aren’t weaponized against activists and journalists
      1. Strengthen Civil Society
      • Support groups that document abuse, provide legal aid, and train citizens on their rights
      • Encourage media to cover protests fairly and avoid harmful stereotypes
VIII. Conclusion: Reclaiming Democratic Space The right to protest is not chaos — it’s democracy in motion. Its how change begins, how governments are held to account, and how people turn pain into purpose. In Nepal and around the world, this right is under siege. But the solution isn’t silence. It’s solidarity. Legal reforms are critical, yes — but so is civic courage. Judges, journalists, lawyers, students, and citizens must all step up. Because the real threat to public order isn’t protest. It’s the erosion of the freedom to protest at all.
post_title: The Right to Protest: Legal Limits and Government Crackdowns – A Global and Nepali Perspective

Pakistan has asked India for the fourth time to rethink its decision to stop the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT). India suspended the treaty after a terrorist attack in Pahalgam on April 22, which killed 26 people.

Pakistan is facing a serious water shortage and is urgently trying to restart the treat. Even after India carried out Operation Sindoor, Pakistan continued to send requests about the treaty.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has made it clear that India will not hold talks while terrorism continues. He said, "Water and blood cannot flow together" and "talks and terror cannot go on at the same time."

Indian government sources say that there are no plans to talk with Pakistan right now, and the treaty will stay suspended.
post_title: Pakistan Begs to India for water

post_content: A 13 years old girl was taken to a hotel raped overnight. The victim's statement is that one of the perpetrators in a group of two, raped her overnight and another person recorded the video. The victim's medical examination report also confirmed that she was raped, and there were marks on her body of syringe that was injected to intoxicate the girl. A complaint was filed at the District Police Office, Siraha, against two people for raping their 13-year-old sister on Bhadra 7, 2080. The complaint alleged that the accused, Pramesh Kumar Yadav and Rajkumar Chaudhary, raped their sister on the pretext of getting her a job. More: Link

post_content: The bench of Honorable Judge Shree Durga Prasad Dhungel has issued a show cause order in the name of Nepal Electricity Authority, Central Office. On Sunday, a law student, Bivek Chaudhary, filed a writ petition in the Patan High Court demanding to give prior notice to the consumers before cutting the electricity. Petitioner has mentioned that Article 27 of our constitution has provisioned for the right to information, and it is the right of the consumers to get prior notice before a power cut.  The petitioner argues that such prior notice would not only uphold consumers' rights but also promote transparency and accountability in the operations of the Nepal Electricity Authority. The hearing of the writ was scheduled on Monday, where Patan High Court issued a show cause order in the name of the defendant. The court has directed the defendant to explain why such notices have not been issued to consumers, emphasizing the importance of transparency and communication in public services. This case could set a significant precedent for consumer rights and accountability in utility management.
post_title: Show Cause order in the name of Nepal Electricity Authority

post_content: Evidence Law: Shahadev Singh Sikh Vs. Others, NKP 2032, No.7, P.175 Case: Homicide Plaintiff: Sundar Singh Sikh Defendant: Shahadev Singh Sikh, Ghirau Singh Sikh, Kunja Bihari Sikh, Badalu Rao Decision Number: 911 This case is related with the principle of evidence law “Who Asserts Must Prove.” Fact of the case: On the date of 2028/02 /22, the plaintiff Sundar Singh Sikh was sleeping alone in his house and his wife (Dukhi Singh) and father (Chheda Singh) had gone to attain marriage ceremony. The defendants Shahadev, Ghirau and two other people came drunk and attacked Sundar Sikh by Khukuri with an intention to kill him but Somehow he managed to save himself. But while Chheda Singh was coming back to home from wedding, the defendants killed him on the way. Sundar Singh Sikh reported in police office, then the defendants admitted that they all were involved in murder that is catching legs by one, striking on face by other, striking khukuri by another, etc. Then the police office filled the case on Banke District Court. Saying that all the defendants must be punished as in 13(1) of Homicide of Muluki Ain. Ratio Decidendi/ Decisions of Court: District Court: There were defendants Shahadev singh, Ghirau Singh, Kunja Bihari and Badalu Rau. There was no real evidence proving that whether all defendants were the principal offender or not. District Court decided that the Shahadev Singh was a principal offender and punished as per 13(1) of homicide. Other offenders rejected their admission made on police office so hence were punished as per 17(2) of homicide. Bheri Zonel Court: The plaintiff Sunder Singh appealed claiming that all offenders should be punished Under 13(1). The defendant Shahadev Singh also appealed claiming that the punishment given to him should be minimized. But, There were no such evidences to prove their claim. Plaintiff and Defendants both cannot produce the evidences to prove their claim. So, the Bheri zonal court also approved the decision of district court. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court had to find out whether the decision of the Zonal Court is right or not? Supreme Court also approved the decision of the Zonal Court on the grounds: It was not mentioned in claim paper about catching legs by  one, striking on face by another, striking Khukuri by another, etc. Only the admission made on police custody cannot be a proof, it must be proved by other proof, then only it can be taken as the basis. Supreme Court asked the defendant that where was he at the time of incident. He claimed that he was in India to buy a machine. The asserting party himself must prove that he was not at the place of incident when it was occurred. But he could not prove. Shahadev has enmity with deceased Chheda and plaintiff Sunder Singh regarding the issue of daughter. In the recognizance , Indicating culprit Shahadev, Dukhi Rana Sikh (plaintiff’s wife) mentioned that she saw Shahadev with Khukuri in his hand, cutting Cheeda neck lying him down on the ground. Almost, all the people of Sarjamin/ground report stated that they’ve doubt on Shahadev on murdering Chheda and disappearing his head. On this basis Division Bench of Supreme Court approved the decision of Bheri Zonal Court.
post_title: Evidence Law Case: Shahadev Singh Sikh Vs. Others, NKP (7th Semester)

Sundar Singh Sikh reported in police office, then the defendants admitted that they all were involved in murder that is catching legs by one, striking on face by other, striking khukuri by another, etc. Then the police office filled the case on Banke District Court. Saying that all the defendants must be punished as in 13(1) of Homicide of Muluki Ain. Ratio Decidendi/ Decisions of Court: District Court: There were defendants Shahadev singh, Ghirau Singh, Kunja Bihari and Badalu Rau. There was no real evidence proving that whether all defendants were the principal offender or not. District Court decided that the Shahadev Singh was a principal offender and punished as per 13(1) of homicide. Other offenders rejected their admission made on police office so hence were punished as per 17(2) of homicide. Bheri Zonel Court: The plaintiff Sunder Singh appealed claiming that all offenders should be punished Under 13(1). The defendant Shahadev Singh also appealed claiming that the punishment given to him should be minimized. But, There were no such evidences to prove their claim. Plaintiff and Defendants both cannot produce the evidences to prove their claim. So, the Bheri zonal court also approved the decision of district court. Supreme Court: The Supreme Court had to find out whether the decision of the Zonal Court is right or not? Supreme Court also approved the decision of the Zonal Court on the grounds: It was not mentioned in claim paper about catching legs by  one, striking on face by another, striking Khukuri by another, etc. Only the admission made on police custody cannot be a proof, it must be proved by other proof, then only it can be taken as the basis. Supreme Court asked the defendant that where was he at the time of incident. He claimed that he was in India to buy a machine. The asserting party himself must prove that he was not at the place of incident when it was occurred. But he could not prove. Shahadev has enmity with deceased Chheda and plaintiff Sunder Singh regarding the issue of daughter. In the recognizance , Indicating culprit Shahadev, Dukhi Rana Sikh (plaintiff’s wife) mentioned that she saw Shahadev with Khukuri in his hand, cutting Cheeda neck lying him down on the ground. Almost, all the people of Sarjamin/ground report stated that they’ve doubt on Shahadev on murdering Chheda and disappearing his head. On this basis Division Bench of Supreme Court approved the decision of Bheri Zonal Court.

A Judge Bhuwan Singh Thapa of Rasuwa district court dragged to Judicial Council investigation after a victim women filed a complaint against the judge thapa. Women who is struggling in the polygamy case claimed that the judge thapa proposed to her through messages and phone calls, asking to spend the night with her. Judge Thapa including a government lawyer dragged to judicial council investigation after they offered a women to spend night with them and a complaint has been filed stating that the judge contacted the litigant with the involvement of the government attorney, aiming to influence the ongoing case and ensure a favorable verdict.

The victim women first filed the complaint at Maiti Nepal, and Maiti Nepal filed complaint to Judicial Council.
